title: Production Observability & Deployment: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on structured logging, metrics, distributed tracing with correlation IDs, health checks, containers and Kubernetes, blue-green and canary releases, and service mesh basics.

chapters.title: Observability Mental Model
points: Three pillars: logs (discrete events), metrics (aggregated numbers over time), traces (one request's path across services); each answers a different question
Monitoring answers known questions (dashboards, alerts); observability lets you ask new questions about unknown failures from rich telemetry
Structured logging: emit JSON with fixed keys (timestamp, level, service, message, trace_id) instead of free text, so logs are queryable and filterable
Metric types: counter (only goes up, use rate()), gauge (up and down, e.g. queue depth), histogram (bucketed values for percentiles)
Choose signals by method: RED for services (Rate, Errors, Duration), USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors)

chapters.title: Tracing, Correlation IDs and Health Checks
points: Correlation ID: a unique ID generated at the edge (or reused from the incoming header) and passed on every downstream call and log line to stitch one request together
Trace = tree of spans; each span has trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, start time and duration
Propagate context via the W3C traceparent header (version-trace_id-parent_id-flags); OpenTelemetry is the standard SDK and export format
Example log line: {"level":"error","service":"orders","trace_id":"4bf92f35","msg":"payment timeout"} lets you jump from a log to its full trace
Liveness vs readiness vs startup probe: liveness failure restarts the container, readiness failure removes it from Service endpoints, startup probe delays the other two until boot finishes
Mistake: dropping the header on async hops (queues, threads) breaks the trace; copy the context into message headers

chapters.title: Containers and Kubernetes Core
points: Container = isolated process sharing the host kernel via namespaces (isolation) and cgroups (resource limits); image = immutable layered filesystem, container = running instance

Kubernetes objects: Pod (smallest unit, one or more containers), Deployment (manages ReplicaSets and rolling updates), Service (stable virtual IP and DNS for pods), Ingress (HTTP routing in), ConfigMap/Secret (config)
Control loop: you declare desired state, controllers reconcile actual state toward it; the scheduler places pods on nodes by resource requests
Requests are used for scheduling, limits are enforced at runtime: exceeding the memory limit gets OOMKilled, exceeding the CPU limit gets throttled
Rolling update (default Deployment strategy): replace pods gradually using maxUnavailable and maxSurge; kubectl rollout undo reverts

chapters.title: Release Strategies: Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary
points: Blue-green: two identical environments, deploy to idle one, test, flip traffic switch (Service selector or load balancer); rollback = flip back; cost is double capacity
Canary: send a small slice (1-5%) of traffic to the new version, watch error rate and latency, then step up to 100% or abort
Comparison: rolling is cheapest but mixes versions with slow rollback; blue-green has instant rollback with all-or-nothing exposure; canary has smallest blast radius but needs good metrics
Automated canary analysis (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) promotes or rolls back from metric thresholds, not human judgement
Mistake: database schema changes break both versions; use expand-and-contract migrations so old and new code both work

chapters.title: Service Mesh Basics and Everyday kubectl
points: Service mesh: a sidecar proxy (Envoy) beside each pod handles service-to-service traffic; the control plane (Istio, Linkerd) pushes config to the proxies
Mesh gives mTLS between services, retries and timeouts, traffic splitting (the weighted routing used for canaries), and uniform metrics and traces without app code changes
Trade-off: extra latency and resource cost per pod, plus operational complexity; skip it for a handful of services

kubectl get pods -o wide, describe pod

(read Events), logs

-f --previous, exec -it

-- sh, apply -f file.yaml, rollout status/undo deployment/
Common failure states: CrashLoopBackOff (app exits, check logs --previous), ImagePullBackOff (bad tag or credentials), Pending (no node fits requests), OOMKilled (raise limit or fix leak)
Mistakes: using the :latest tag, no resource requests or limits, a liveness probe that checks dependencies (causes restart storms), logging to files instead of stdout

chapters.title: Production Observability Cheat Sheet
points: Signals: logs = what happened, metrics = how much and how often, traces = where time went; RED for services, USE for resources
Correlation: traceparent header in, trace_id in every log line, copied into async message headers
Probes: liveness restarts, readiness removes from traffic, startup gates the others
Releases: rolling = cheap and mixed versions, blue-green = instant flip and 2x cost, canary = small blast radius and needs metrics
Debug order: kubectl get, describe (Events), logs --previous, exec; rollback with rollout undo
